title: Private Deployments: Attestation & Provisioning — Arch Review
content:
Meeting: Private Deployments Architecture Review — Attestation & Provisioning
Date: 2026-02-18
Location: Zoom + #eng-private-deployments (thread tidied into PR comments)
Attendees: Amina (owner), Diego, Priya, Jonah, Marisol, Riley, (observing: security PO)
Objective: Decide on a pragmatic attestation-and-provisioning design for Private (VPC + on-prem) that balances: security (verifiable boot/root of trust), operational simplicity for SEs, and compatibility with offline/on-prem air-gapped installs.

Background / motivation:
- Customers deploying Redwood Private require cryptographic proof that the runtime image they received originates from Redwood and hasn't been tampered with. Many ask for an attestation flow that integrates with their KMS/HSM and existing inventory systems.
- Previous proposals split between: (1) full-blown remote attestation via TPM/SGX + central Redwood CA; (2) image-signatures + offline verification during install; (3) a hybrid where ephemeral enrollment tokens retrieve signed assertions from Redwood after on-prem bootstrap.
- Constraints: air-gapped installs (no outbound connectivity), minimal friction for on-prem SEs, audit trail for enterprise compliance.

Agenda summary:
1) Quick run-through of threat model and constraints (Priya)
2) Present three shortlisted designs (Diego)
3) Tradeoffs & integration points with Private Console + Installer (Jonah)
4) Compatability with customer KMS (Marisol)
5) Decision, action items, owners, and follow-ups (Amina)

Threat model highlights (abridged):
- Adversary: malicious actor with file-system access to a node before boot, or supply-chain tampering of images.
- We must provide: proof of image provenance, detect unauthorized changes to runtime binary or model artifacts, and ensure enrollment keys are not trivially re-playable.
- We assume customers may require proof of both code provenance (signatures) and environment integrity (hardware-based attestation where available).

Shortlisted designs presented
Design A — Image-signature-first, optional hardware attestation:
- Flow: Image artifacts are signed by Redwood (detached sigs). Installer verifies signatures during install against embedded Redwood CA cert. Optionally, if host has TPM, a PCR-based quote is performed and attached to installation metadata pushed to customer S3/console.
- Pros: Works in air-gapped installs; simple; minimal external dependencies; easy manual audit.
- Cons: Limited runtime integrity guarantees after install; weaker against privileged local tampering post-install without hardware-backed attestation enabled.

Design B — Enrollment token + remote assertion (default for hosted-capable sites):
- Flow: Installer uses a short-lived enrollment token (generated in Redwood Console) to authenticate to Redwood-managed attestation-service over TLS, performs a nonce exchange, and receives a signed attestation object covering image digest, node-id, and enrollment timestamp. Tokens are single-use, expire within 5 minutes.
- Pros: Provides a strong, auditable server-side assertion; centralized logging; supports revocation if token compromised.
- Cons: Not possible for air-gapped; requires customer networking policy to allow outbound to attestation endpoints (can be proxied).

Design C — Hardware-rooted remote attestation (TPM / Intel TDX / AMD SEV):
- Flow: On supported hardware, the installer orchestrates a TPM/TDX attestation flow producing a signed quote which Redwood (or a customer Relying Party) verifies against the expected measurement set (image digest + runtime checks).
- Pros: Strongest guarantee for runtime integrity; high assurance for regulated customers.
- Cons: Complex cross-vendor support; longer implementation ramp; requires hardware support and sometimes kernel config changes; less friendly for quick SE installs.

Discussion notes (key points raised)
- Priya: For many customers, Design A will satisfy policy because they combine signed images with host-level config management (Chef/Puppet). But auditors increasingly ask for continuous attestation, not just at install.
- Diego: Hybrid approach (A as baseline + automated token-based assertion when connectivity allowed) gives best coverage across customer types.
- Jonah: The console UX must make generation of enrollment tokens frictionless for SEs — short-lives and single-use reduces blast radius. Also need a way to bind token to an installer run (nonce or ephemeral keypair).
- Marisol: KMS integrations — the attestation service should support both Redwood-managed keys (default) and customer-managed keys (BYOK). BYOK for signing is a must for some regulated customers.
- Riley: For air-gapped customers we should provide an 'offline assertion bundle' — a signed metadata package including image digest and verifier instructions that customers can import into their internal PKI.

Decision (consensus):
- Proceed with a two-track implementation: Baseline = Design A (Image signatures + offline assertion bundle) for air-gapped and quick installs; Primary track = Hybrid (Design B) where enrollment tokens + server-side assertions are used when outbound connectivity is available.
- Hardware-based remote attestation (Design C) to be treated as an advanced feature (Phase 2) with a separate RFC due in Q3 2026.

Concrete design decisions and constraints to capture in RFC (action: Amina + Diego):
- Image signing format: use CMS (RFC 5652) detached signatures, with a small manifest JSON that includes image digest (sha256), build id, provenance URL, and optional manifest of included system packages.
- Installer verifies detached signature against embedded Redwood root cert. Installer returns a simple verification status code and writes verification metadata to /var/lib/redwood/attestation.json (human-readable + machine readable).
- Enrollment token flow: tokens minted in Console with scope: {customer-id, installer-version, max-uses=1, expires_in=300s}. Installer must generate ephemeral keypair and produce a CSR signed by the ephemeral key; Redwood returns an attestation object signed by Redwood KMS key.
- Offline assertion bundle: CLI tool to produce bundle signed by Redwood; includes instructions to import into local PKI and verification script (sh).
- BYOK: Support HSM-backed signing via templates in the attestation-service; initial scope: AWS KMS & Azure Key Vault. GCP KMS later.

Operational / UX decisions (action: Jonah + Priya):
- Console: Add "Create enrollment token" flow with optional allowlist by CIDR and installer version check. Tokens surfaced with copy-to-clipboard and QR for SE use.
- Installer: Verbose mode to emit attestation metadata and friendly troubleshooting messages.
- SRE: Attestation service requires HA across two regions; log retention 90 days for audit (configurable per customer).

Open questions (to be resolved in RFC or follow-ups):
- How do we bind an enrollment token to a particular installer run to prevent token theft and replay in non-air-gapped but insecure networks? (short-term: ephemeral keypair CSR binding; long-term: TPM-based key attestation)
- What format do customers prefer for the offline bundle verification script? POSIX sh only or include PowerShell? (action: Marisol to survey top 10 enterprise customers)
- Re: BYOK — what adoption threshold makes it worth building vault-plugin hooks for non-cloud HSMs? (action: Amina to triage requests through sales).

Action items (owner — ETA):
- Draft RFC: "Attestation & Provisioning for Private" (Amina + Diego) — 2026-03-05
- Prototype CLI: offline-assertion-bundle generator (Jonah) — 2026-03-19
- Console token UX mockups + small validation test in staging (Priya) — 2026-03-12
- KMS/BYOK initial spec (Marisol) — 2026-03-22
- Small internal PoC: enrollment-token flow (Riley + Diego) — 2026-03-26
- Security review kickoff with compliance (Priya) — 2026-02-25

Follow-ups / next meeting:
- RFC review workshop scheduled: 2026-03-10, 10:00 PT (deep dive on manifest fields and signature format)
- PoC demo readout: 2026-03-26 (sync with SEs and sales for feedback)

Appendix (implementation hints and examples)
- Example manifest (proposed fields):
  {
    "image_sha256": "<hex>",
    "build_id": "rbw-2026-02-10-rc3",
    "packages": ["libc 2.35", "rt-runtime 1.9.2"],
    "timestamp": "2026-02-18T15:22:00Z",
    "installer_version": "0.12.1"
  }

- Example minimal installer verification command (posix):
  # ./redwood-install --verify /path/to/image.tar.gz --sig /path/to/image.sig 
  # writes /var/lib/redwood/attestation.json with status and signed-manifest

- Enrollment token sequence (high level):
  1) Console: mint token with scope and expiry
  2) Installer: generate ephemeral keypair, produce CSR including nonce from token
  3) Attestation service: validate token, verify CSR, return signed attestation blob including image digest + timestamp
  4) Installer: write attestation blob to disk and surface to admin

Notes on security posture:
- Use short-lived tokens and single-use semantics to reduce blast radius.
- Signatures must be verifiable offline via root cert; support rotation via intermediate signing certs and publish CRL/OCSP endpoints for online setups.
- Logs must include installer fingerprint (ephemeral public key) so revocation investigations can tie an assertion to a run.

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Customer misuse of offline bundle could allow stale assertions to be reused. Mitigation: include timestamp + recommended max-age and encourage switching to token flow when connectivity is available.
- Risk: BYOK complexity delays launch. Mitigation: ship with Redwood-managed keys and a BYOK roadmap; prioritize AWS & Azure KV first.

End notes:
- This doc will be turned into RFC-0 (Draft) and attached to JIRA-PDP-1148; please comment inline on the RFC draft when available.
- If you have platform-level objections (SRE or infra constraints) call out in-line in the RFC or ping Amina directly.

Recorded decisions (short):
- Baseline: detached image signatures + offline bundle (air-gapped-friendly).
- Primary: enrollment-token + server-side attestation for connected installs.
- Phase 2: hardware-rooted attestation (RFC separately).

Prepared by: Amina N. Rahman
